notes: One entry per posting day. 'caption' is an array of paragraphs joined with blank lines at publish time. 'source_material' records provenance for original lines and is never displayed; it exists so the record of which words are Lee's stays intact. 'status' is pending until the daily workflow publishes it.

posts.text: Love is the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real.
posts.source: Iris Murdoch, "The Sublime and the Good", Chicago Review 13:3 (Autumn 1959)
caption: Murdoch calls it difficult and she means it literally. Not difficult like a virtue is difficult. Difficult like a fact you keep having to re-learn.

Most of the time other people run as scenery. Obstacles in traffic, names in an inbox, the person ahead of you taking too long. It costs nothing to treat them that way, which is exactly why it is the default.

The realisation she describes is the moment that collapses. Not sympathy. Registration. The person in front of you is running the same full-colour, first-person, unbearably specific thing you are, right now, and has been all along.
Who did you treat as scenery this week who was not scenery?

posts.text: Taking more than you give is not a personality trait. It is a transfer, and someone else is paying for it.
posts.source_material: Lee's foundational challenge 3: routine participation is moral if you put back as much as you receive; taking more than one gives is unjust.
caption: Reciprocity is the least fashionable idea in this framework and the one that does the most work.

The claim is not that every exchange must balance. It is structural: no one's capacity for experience should be systematically diminished to sustain someone else's. A quiet life that puts back roughly what it takes out is entirely just. A large life that runs a permanent deficit against other people is not, however impressive it looks.
This is also what stops the framework collapsing into self-improvement. Maximizing your own experience at the cost of someone else's is not a stronger version of the idea. It is the failure case.
What are you currently taking that you have not accounted for?

posts.text: It is okay to be inconvenient. It is very human to be so. No one asked to be here.
posts.source_material: Close to Lee's own wording, 9/12/24 journal entry on spontaneous visits.
caption: There is a particular cowardice that looks like consideration.

You are near a friend's house. You do not stop, because they might be busy, might have company, might not want you. So you drive past, and you call it respect for their time. What it actually is, most of the time, is an unwillingness to find out where you stand.

Every outcome of stopping is information. They are glad, and you both got something. They are busy but warm, and you learned the friendship survives bad timing. They are put off, and now you know something real that you would otherwise have spent years not knowing.
The vulnerability is the point. Not the visit.
When did you last decide not to bother someone, and what were you actually protecting?

posts.text: Indifference is not neutral once you have power. From there, doing nothing is a thing you did.
posts.source_material: Lee's foundational challenge 7: indifference is mostly neutral until tied to power or harm, at which point those who do care are obligated to act.
caption: Not caring is usually harmless. A person indifferent to something they cannot affect has done nothing wrong.

Power changes the arithmetic. Once your inaction is load-bearing, once someone's options actually narrow because you declined to move, indifference stops being an absence and becomes a decision with a cost attached to someone else.

The obligation is not unlimited, and this framework is careful about that. It scales with four things: how close you are, what you are actually capable of, how badly the other person is being constricted, and whether acting would work. You are not required to solve everything.
You are required not to be the reason someone has less.
Where do you hold more power than you usually admit?

posts.text: You have never once touched the world. You have touched the report of it, and found the report worth having.
caption: Everything you have ever called direct contact arrived as a signal.

Light hits the retina and becomes voltage. Pressure on skin becomes voltage. Somewhere behind your eyes the voltage becomes the smell of rain, the weight of a hand, the specific colour of a particular afternoon. You have never been outside that process. Nobody has.

This is usually delivered as bad news, a kind of imprisonment. It does not have to be. The report is not a lesser thing standing in for the real one. The report is where every good hour of your life actually took place, and it is the one thing you cannot doubt is happening.
What did your senses hand you this week that you would not trade?

posts.text: Have patience with everything unresolved in your heart. Try to love the questions themselves.
posts.source: Rainer Maria Rilke, Letters to a Young Poet, Letter Four (written 1903, published 1929), trans. Stephen Mitchell (1984)
caption: Rilke was twenty-seven, writing to a nineteen year old who wanted to be told what to do.
He refuses. Love the questions themselves, he says, like locked rooms or books in a foreign language. Do not go looking for answers, because you could not live them yet.

That advice softens into a greeting card very easily. It is actually hard. Loving a question means giving up the relief of closing it, and closing things is most of what a mind wants to do. The framework this account is built on makes the same demand less gently: we cannot know what matters, and that is the finding, not a stage on the way to a finding.
Which open question are you trying to close early?

posts.text: The good things are not free. They cost perspective. You have to know how bad it gets to know what you have.
posts.source_material: Close to Lee's own wording, 9/13/24: the good things in life aren't free, they come at the cost of perspective.
caption: This is where the framework parts company with almost every philosophy of calm.

It does not treat suffering as something to be transcended, minimized, or seen through. It treats contrast as the mechanism by which anything gets assessed at all. Without variety you have no scale, and without a scale you cannot tell a good hour from a flat one. You would just be somewhere.
Which is why a paradise defined by the absence of discomfort is not obviously desirable. Remove everything that hurt and you remove the instrument you were measuring with.
None of this makes suffering good. Most of it is waste. The claim is narrower and stranger: the capacity to be hurt is part of the same equipment as the capacity to be moved.
What good thing in your life would not register without something difficult behind it?

posts.text: Every person you passed today is the center of a world as vivid as this one. Almost none of them are extras.
caption: The default setting is that you are the protagonist and everyone else is atmosphere. It is not arrogance, it is architecture. You have access to exactly one inside.
But the inference to other minds is a small one, not a large one. Same body, same nervous system, same reports of the same world. Doubting it takes more machinery than accepting it.

The driver in the next lane has a childhood, a worst day, an unfinished argument, a song that ruins them. Running at full volume, right now, three metres away, with no more access to your inside than you have to theirs.
When did you last catch yourself realising a stranger was a whole person?

posts.text: You did not build the road you drove in on. Reciprocity is noticing that, and then behaving as if it is true.
posts.source_material: Lee's foundational challenge 9: institutions should protect against exploitation of labour, time, energy and shared resources.
caption: Almost everything that makes your day possible was made by someone you will never meet and did not pay directly.

The road, the grid, the water, the language you are reading this in, the accumulated medical knowledge that means a childhood infection did not end you. You inherited a working commons. Nobody earns that.

The framework does not turn this into guilt. It turns it into arithmetic. If your capacity to experience anything at all rests on a commons, then systematically drawing that commons down for your own benefit is not clever. It is the one clearly unjust move available.
Which is why this idea has consequences most personal philosophies avoid. About hoarding. About labour. About who is paying for your convenience.
What did you use today that you did not build and have not replaced?

posts.text: Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.
posts.source: Simone Weil, letter to Joë Bousquet, 13 April 1942 (in Weil's Correspondance; cited in Simone Pétrement, Simone Weil: A Life, 1976). Frequently misattributed to Gravity and Grace.
caption: This line is almost always credited to Gravity and Grace. It is not from there. It comes from a letter Weil wrote to the poet Joë Bousquet in April 1942, which somehow makes it better.

Her claim is stronger than it first sounds. Not that attention is generous, but that it is the rarest form of generosity. Rarer than money, rarer than time. Anyone can be in a room. Very few people are in it with you.
You feel the difference the moment you receive it, and you feel its absence just as fast. Being listened to by someone waiting for their turn to talk is not being listened to.
It is also costly in the way this framework cares about. Real attention means being changed by what you find, which is why most of us ration it.
Who gave you their actual attention recently, and did you tell them it registered?

posts.text: Consent, context, intent. If you cannot answer all three, you are not helping. You are deciding for someone.
posts.source_material: Lee's CCI test, developed through foundational challenge 2.
caption: Most harm done in good faith passes two of these and fails the third quietly.

Consent: did they agree, and could they have refused without cost? Context: is this actually a situation where growth is plausible, or are you assuming that? Intent: are you trying to expand what is available to them, or to resolve something in yourself?

The test does not need all three to be perfect. It needs you to be able to answer them. Where you cannot, you have stopped acting with a person and started acting on one, and the fact that you meant well is not a defence they have to accept.
It is a deliberately unglamorous test. That is the point. It is meant to be usable on a Tuesday, not admired.
Is it sufficient though? Foreseeable consequences, competence, the ability to withdraw later. Which would you add?

posts.text: A camera perceives light and captures the moment. It does not experience the moment. Perception was never the whole of it.
posts.source_material: Lee's own analogy from the is-ought work: a camera perceives light and images and moments but does not have the same value, because it captures a fragment without experiencing it.
caption: This is a correction to the framework's own foundation, and it matters.

The starting claim is usually stated as: perception is the only thing you cannot doubt. But a camera perceives. A thermostat perceives. Neither is the kind of thing anything can matter to. What survives doubt is not sensation arriving somewhere. It is sensation arriving somewhere that registers it is arriving.

Perception plus understanding. The second half does most of the work, and it changes who is inside the circle. The question stops being what can detect, and becomes what can be a subject of its own detecting.
It also makes the hard part harder. Understanding is clearly not binary. A dog, an infant, someone surfacing from anaesthesia.
Where would you put the minimum threshold, and on what evidence?

posts.text: You can act without knowing. You have been doing it every single day since you were born.
caption: The standard objection to holding uncertainty is that it is paralysing. You cannot live without answers, so pick some.

Except you already live without them, constantly, and it does not paralyse you at all. You do not know whether the marriage lasts, whether the job holds, whether the body cooperates, whether the person you are counting on is still there in ten years. You proceed anyway. You have never done anything else.
So the question was never whether action requires certainty. It is why you demand certainty for the large questions when you have never once required it for the ones you actually live by.
Where are you waiting for proof before you will commit?

posts.text: A life arranged to avoid all discomfort has nothing left to measure itself against.
posts.source_material: Derived from Lee's rejection of any ideal state defined by the absence of difficulty.
caption: Comfort is not the enemy. Most of the effort of being alive goes into securing enough of it, and that effort is not a mistake.

The problem is comfort as a governing aim. Optimize hard enough for the absence of friction and you get a life with no contrast in it, which is not peace. It is a flat signal. You stop being able to tell the good days apart, because there is nothing to tell them apart from.
This is a claim about instruments, not about virtue. Difficulty is not ennobling. It is just the only thing that gives the scale its markings.
What have you optimized out of your life that you might actually want back?

posts.text: Cruelty requires forgetting that the other one is also awake. That is all it has ever required.
caption: Almost nobody experiences themselves as cruel. That is the part worth sitting with.

The mechanism is not malice, it is downgrade. The other person becomes a category, a position, an account number, a problem. Once they are a category, everything that follows feels reasonable, because categories do not have Tuesday mornings and people they are worried about.

Which is oddly hopeful if you take it seriously. The correction is not becoming a better person in some general way. It is much smaller and much more repeatable. Remember the other one is awake. Then respond.
Where in your life is it currently convenient to think of someone as a category?

posts.text: Kindness is a currency. The only real question is whether you are earning it or spending down someone else's.
posts.source_material: Lee's 9/16/24 topic list: kindness as a currency.
caption: Treating kindness as an economy sounds cynical until you notice that people already do.

Every group has someone reliably generous, and someone quietly running on the generosity of others without replenishing it. Both are visible. Neither is usually named. The second one is often perfectly pleasant, which is exactly what makes the imbalance easy to sustain.

The framework's version of the test is not who is nicest. It is whether anyone's capacity is being systematically drawn down to keep someone else comfortable. That happens between friends, in families, and at the scale of whole economies, and it is the same failure each time.
Who in your life is currently subsidising someone, and does anyone say so?

posts.text: Fighting every signal telling you not to say you love someone, and saying it anyway.
posts.source_material: Close to Lee's own wording, 9/13/24, from the passage describing what he would actually count as paradise.
caption: There is a whole system in you built to prevent this. It is fast, it is articulate, and it will supply a dozen good reasons in the time it takes to breathe in.
Wrong moment. They know already. It will be strange afterwards. You will have changed something you cannot change back.
That last one is true, which is why the system works so well. Saying it does move you somewhere you cannot return from. Every meaningful thing does.

The framework does not treat this as sentiment. It treats it as the practice. The small deliberate act of accepting exposure in exchange for something real, rather than staying safe and calling it timing.
Who have you not said it to, and what reason have you been giving yourself?

posts.text: You are not obligated to fix everything. You are obligated not to be the reason someone else has less.
posts.source_material: Lee's position across foundational challenges 7 and 9, plus the obligation-scaling analysis.
caption: The usual objection to demanding ethics is that they are impossible. If every suffering makes a claim on me then I fail immediately and permanently, so why start.

This framework does not make that claim. The floor is negative and specific: do not actively constrict what is available to other people. That is achievable by anyone, on any given day, and most people mostly manage it.

The positive obligation is real but bounded. It scales with how close you are, what you can actually do, how severe the constriction is, and whether acting would work at all. Which means it lands differently on a bystander than on someone holding the relevant power, and that asymmetry is the entire point.
You are allowed to have a life. You are not allowed to build it on someone else's narrowed one.
Where is the line between not solving something and being part of why it persists?

posts.text: I am, I exist, is necessarily true whenever it is put forward by me or conceived in my mind.
posts.source: René Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy (1641), Meditation II, trans. John Cottingham (1984)
caption: Descartes had just finished dismantling everything. The senses could be lying. The world could be fabricated. A powerful deceiver could be running the whole show.

Then he finds the floor. Whatever else is false, something is doing the doubting, and the doubting is occurring. It survives every attack he can invent, and he notices it is exactly one fact, no larger.
Note how little it gives him. Not a world, not a body, not another person. Just: this is happening, and it is happening to something that can tell.
Nearly four centuries later that is still the only item on the list. Everything this account posts is an attempt to work out what follows from one fact.
If that is the single certainty available, what would you build on it?

posts.text: And as for certain truth, no man has seen it, nor will there ever be a man who knows.
posts.source: Xenophanes, Fragment 34 (DK 21B34), trans. Kathleen Freeman, Ancilla to the Pre-Socratic Philosophers (1948). Quoted in part; the fragment continues "...about the gods and about all the things I mention. For even if a man should chance to say most exactly what is true, still he himself knows not that it is so."
caption: Someone worked this out roughly two and a half thousand years ago and we have not meaningfully improved on it.

The second half of the fragment is the part that stings. Even if a man should chance to say exactly what is true, Xenophanes writes, still he knows not that it is so. Being right is not the same as knowing you are right, and there is no internal signal separating them.
Which means confidence was never evidence. It is a feeling, and it feels identical whether or not you happen to be correct.
The move this framework makes from there is not despair. Unknowability is a finding about meaning, not about experience. Something is still happening, and that fact is still on the table.
What are you most certain about with no way to check?

posts.text: Nothing about this is guaranteed to mean anything. Notice that you went ahead and loved people anyway.
caption: The argument usually runs one direction. If there is no guaranteed meaning then nothing matters, and everything collapses.

But that is a prediction, and it has been tested continuously by every person who lost their certainty and got up the next morning regardless. The prediction fails. People keep showing up for each other with no metaphysical backing whatsoever, and it does not look like a mistake.
Which suggests the caring was never downstream of the certainty. It was managing fine on its own the whole time. The certainty was just taking the credit.
This is the whole framework compressed. You cannot know what it is for, something is nonetheless happening, and what you do about that is available to you right now.
Who do you love without a reason that would survive scrutiny?
